turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late. The tram sat at Richmond for ages and then I got the wrong lift.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): No worries. Take a second, we've still got time.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. Bit warm out, I legged it from the stop.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. What brought you in?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): It's nothing, honestly. I nearly didn't come. Just the heel.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): The heel. Tell me about it, even if you reckon it's minor.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Right one. First thing, those first steps, it nips, then it walks off. Not a big deal.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, six weeks. No, hang on, it started before the long weekend, so closer to two months.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): So two months, right heel, worst on the first steps, then it settles. Have I got that straight?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. I can still do a full shift though.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): What sort of shift is it?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Hardware shop. On my feet the whole day, up and down the aisles. I run three times a week as well, nothing flash.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have new shoes been part of this?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh, umm, yeah. New joggers about a month ago. Flat as. Thought they'd be fine.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Does the running stir the heel up?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): A bit after, maybe. Morning's worse than the running. I'm not giving it up.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any swelling or redness that you've seen?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Nah. Looks normal. My boss reckons I limp, but I don't.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or pins and needles in the foot?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): How's your breathing when you run?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Fine. Lungs are good.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are you taking any tablets, even the odd one?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Not really. Neurofen if it annoys me. Two hundred mils, nah, the tablets are four hundred. Just one.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): And how often would that be?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Couple of times a week. I forget half the time. Not worth fussing.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, neurofen included?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): Nah. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has the heel been scanned before?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Ultrasound, ages ago. Couldn't tell you when, last year or maybe before. They said the fascia was borderline thick. I left it.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): An old ultrasound, called borderline thick, no actual figure, and you didn't chase it. Mind if I have a feel?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): Go on. You won't find much.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tender just in front of the right heel pad. No swelling, the skin isn't red, and the calf feels tight.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): See. Hardly a thing.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think this is most likely plantar fasciitis. The morning first-step pain and that tender spot fit, and we don't need a scan today.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): So I just put up with it then?

[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stretch the calf and the sole before you get out of bed, morning and night. Grab some cushioned insoles from the chemist, and give those flat joggers a rest on the long shifts. If it's still niggling in six weeks, come back and see me.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Stretches and insoles. Heaps of fuss for a small niggle.

spec.situation: Runner or shop worker with heel pain on the first steps in the morning for two months; new shoes mentioned; doctor suggests stretches and insoles; no tests.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
